title: Ezekiel 23:1–10
context: The prophet reports that the LORD’s word came to him, and the LORD addresses him as “son of man” and tells an allegory of two sisters, daughters of one mother, named Oholah and Oholibah, and explains, “Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem Oholibah.” Using the chapter’s strong imagery of unfaithfulness, the LORD describes Oholah (Samaria) turning from him to Egypt in her youth and then to Assyria, and handing her over to the Assyrians she had pursued, a picture of the northern kingdom’s fall (cf. 2 Kgs 17:4–6). Both traditions read the allegory as shared ground about covenant unfaithfulness through political alliances and idolatry, and they name Ezekiel 16 and Jeremiah 3:6–11 as related passages without harmonizing them.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came again to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s word came again to me, saying.” Arminian readers note that the prophet introduces a new word from the LORD.

The chapter is the LORD speaking to Ezekiel, who is to declare it to the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet receiving and reporting the LORD’s message.

Shared ground: both traditions read the opening as marking a prophetic word, and both prepare to read what follows as allegory rather than as a literal account of two women.

verses.text: “Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.” Arminian readers note that “son of man” is Ezekiel’s usual title in the book (cf. 2:1).

The two sisters share one origin, a picture of the one people later divided into two kingdoms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the title as a reminder of the prophet’s humanity before God, not as a point of disagreement.

Shared ground: both traditions read the two women as an allegory for Israel and Judah, as 23:4 will explain.

verses.text: They played the prostitute in Egypt. They played the prostitute in their youth. Their breasts were fondled there, and their youthful nipples were caressed there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes the sisters’ unfaithfulness beginning in Egypt, in strong figurative language. Arminian readers note that the allegory traces Israel’s idolatry back to its time in Egypt (cf. 20:7–8).

The imagery is figurative and should be read soberly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the allegory portraying a long history of turning from the LORD.

Shared ground: both traditions describe this verse in general terms, without repeating its imagery, and read it as a picture of covenant unfaithfulness rooted in the nation’s earliest days.

verses.text: Their names were Oholah the elder, and Oholibah her sister. They became mine, and they bore sons and daughters. As for their names, Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem Oholibah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Their names were Oholah the elder, and Oholibah her sister.” Arminian readers note that the LORD explains the allegory: “Samaria is Oholah, and Jerusalem Oholibah.”

The names are often linked to the word for “tent,” though their exact sense is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the meaning of the names lightly while affirming the identification the text itself gives.

Shared ground: both traditions note the words “They became mine,” which frame the whole allegory as a covenant relationship the sisters betrayed.

verses.text: “Oholah played the prostitute when she was mine. She doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbors,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Oholah turned to her lovers, “the Assyrians her neighbors.” Arminian readers note that the allegory turns to Samaria’s alliances with Assyria.

Political dependence is portrayed as unfaithfulness to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see reliance on foreign powers as a betrayal of trust in God.

Shared ground: both traditions read the “lovers” as the nations Samaria relied on, and agree that the allegory’s concern is covenant loyalty, not a literal story.

verses.text: who were clothed with blue—governors and rulers, all of them desirable young men, horsemen riding on horses.
verses.arminianNotes:
Samaria’s “lovers” are described as “governors and rulers” and “horsemen riding on horses.” Arminian readers note the attraction of Assyrian power and splendor.

The image explains why Samaria was drawn to Assyria.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the appeal of worldly strength that tempted the northern kingdom.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the verse depicts the lure of military and political power that drew God’s people away from trusting him.

verses.text: She gave herself as a prostitute to them, all of them the choicest men of Assyria. She defiled herself with the idols of whomever she lusted after.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Samaria “defiled herself with the idols” of the nations she pursued. Arminian readers note that political alliance and idolatry are joined.

Alliances with Assyria brought foreign worship with them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see idolatry as the deeper offense beneath the political choices.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that trusting the nations led Samaria to worship their idols, which the LORD names as defilement.

verses.text: She hasn’t left her prostitution since leaving Egypt; for in her youth they lay with her. They caressed her youthful nipples and they poured out their prostitution on her.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that Samaria has not left the unfaithfulness she began in Egypt, using the chapter’s strong imagery. Arminian readers note the theme of persistent sin across generations.

They describe the verse in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a long pattern of turning from the LORD.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, without repeating its imagery, as a statement that Samaria’s unfaithfulness was not new but long rooted (cf. 2 Kgs 17:7).

verses.text: “Therefore I delivered her into the hand of her lovers, into the hand of the Assyrians on whom she doted.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore I delivered her into the hand of her lovers, into the hand of the Assyrians.” Arminian readers note that the LORD hands Samaria over to the power she trusted.

This matches the fall of Samaria to Assyria (2 Kgs 17:6).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment working through the nations.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that sin’s consequences come through the very things trusted in place of God, and they keep the existing box at Judges 9:23 in view rather than adding one.

verses.text: These uncovered her nakedness. They took her sons and her daughters, and they killed her with the sword. She became a byword among women; for they executed judgments on her.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes Samaria’s shame and fall in strong allegorical terms, and her children taken. Arminian readers read this as a picture of the northern kingdom’s destruction and exile.

The imagery is figurative and is described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly as the end of the northern kingdom.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Samaria “became a byword among women,” and read the allegory as the nation’s fall, not as a pattern for how any person should be treated.
